newsitem.title: USA: Dollar soars as Japan, France endorse strong dollar.
newsitem.headline: Dollar soars as Japan, France endorse strong dollar.

text.p: The dollar rose against major currencies on Wednesday after officials from Japan and France aligned themselves with the U.S. position favouring a strong dollar.

The dollar reached a 46-month high against the Japanese yen and a 31-month peak against the German mark after Japan's finance minister and the head of France's central bank said the Group of Seven nations backed U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin's exchange rate policy.
Rubin restated his well-known preference for a strong dollar on Tuesday.
"The United States is calling the shots now," said Jeffrey Yu, senior dealer at Sanwa Bank in New York.

"European central banks are very happy the dollar is higher. Japan, in the beginning, was worried about weakness of yen translating to weaker Nikkei stocks, but it seems like everybody is thinking differently now."

The dollar rose to 119.03 yen late Wednesday from 117.91 yen late Tuesday, and to 1.6421 marks from 1.6296 marks. It also set a 32-month high of 1.4360 Swiss francs, before settling at 1.4295, up from 1.4180 Swiss francs late Tuesday.
Investors interpreted a comment from Japanese Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka as a signal to buy dollars against yen.

Although he said the pace of recent developments in the currency markets has been "rather fast," Mitsuzuka backed away from recent calls against excessive yen weakness by saying the G7 accepts the U.S. stance on the dollar, traders said.
Bank of France Governor Jean-Claude Trichet expressed similar sentiments on the part of the G7 in a newspaper article, which boosted the dollar against the mark.

The dollar later succumbed to mild profit-taking while U.S. stocks and bonds fell sharply. The Dow Jones industrial average fell 33.87 points to close at 6,850.03 Wednesday, partially offsetting Tuesday's 40-point advance.
The benchmark 30-year Treasury bond fell 17/32, raising its yield to 6.83 percent from 6.79 percent Tuesday. The yield and the price move in opposite directions.
"When stocks go down, they try to push (the dollar) lower, but in the end I think the dollar against Europe is going higher," Yu said.

Comments from Bundesbank Council Member Ernst Welteke also weighed on the dollar after the German central bank official told journalists in Frankfurt the mark's slide could not continue "at the pace at which it had been going."
However, Welteke also said the weak mark posed no threat to the German economy or its stable inflation rate. By the close of trade, the dollar had overcome his mild warnings about the weak mark.
"He's talking out both sides of his mouth," said John Gariano, vice president at Sumitomo Bank in New York.
"Even though it's going to fuel some of their overseas export growth ... some of their imports are going to be higher in price now due to the fact the dollar is getting stonger."
Elsewhere, the surging dollar pushed the British pound down to $1.6343 from $1.6635 late Tuesday. The dollar closed at Canadian $1.3373, up from C$1.3367.
